## Defining alerting rules

The optional `for` clause causes Prometheus to wait for a certain duration
between first encountering a new expression output vector element and counting
an alert as firing for this element. In this case, Prometheus will check that
the alert continues to be active during each evaluation for 10 minutes before
firing the alert. Elements that are active, but not firing yet, are in the pending state.
Alerting rules without the `for` clause will become active on the first evaluation.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md:15" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/the_zen.md" title="The Zen of Prometheus" section="The Zen of Prometheus > Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

For more context My Philosophy on Alerting.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

## Symptom-based alerts for paging, cause-based for troubleshooting

Similar to Measure what users care about, alert on what *really* matters. It doesn't matter if your CPU is saturated, as long as your users don't notice. Let your SLOs guide your alerting.

Not every alert needs to page someone. Cause-based alerts shouldn't wake anyone up—they should feed into dashboards or ticket queues to be checked when needed or handled in batches at leisure. Reserve paging for symptom-based alerts that indicate user-facing impact.

For more context My Philosophy on Alerting.
</source>

## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.

</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. <source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D04:4" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Who to contact" date="2026-02-14" type="official">

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D13:0" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Monthly limit" date="2026-09-01" type="official">

</source>

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

## When does it not fit?

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are
available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100%
accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as
the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a
case, you would be best off using some other system to collect and analyze the
data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring.
</source>

The agent platform is the set of services our agents run on. Agents are configured in the registry, look things up through shared services, and are watched by monitoring. ### Features

Prometheus's main features are:

* a multi-dimensional data model with time series data identified by metric name and key/value pairs
* PromQL, a flexible query language

* no reliance on distributed storage; single server nodes are autonomous
* time series collection happens via a pull model over HTTP
* pushing time series is supported via an intermediary gateway
* targets are discovered via service discovery or static configuration
* multiple modes of graphing and dashboarding support
</source>

Based on my search of the documentation and incident records, here's what I found about agent dependencies on auth-service:

**All agents** are affected by auth-service failures. According to the architecture overview [D04:2], when a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header before reading or writing registry-db. Since all agents interact with registry-api, an auth-service outage would slow down or block all agent requests.

Additionally, the **billing_agent** has an additional specific dependency on auth-service. During incident INC-2041 [D09:2], the billing_agent experienced issues when auth-service's certificate expired, which caused payments-gateway (a service used by billing_agent) to fail certificate checks. This led to billing_agent being unable to issue invoices.

**Note:** The agent platform architecture overview states: "It doesn't cover every service an individual agent uses; each agent's owner documents those." So while all agents depend on auth-service through registry-api, individual agents may have additional private dependencies documented with their owners.

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.

## When does it not fit?

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are
available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100%
accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as
the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a

data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring.

Prometheus's main features are:

## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

content.text:
Based on my research of the documentation and incident records, here's what I found about agents that stop working if auth-service goes down:

**From the documentation:**
- `auth-service` validates registry keys and issues internal certificates that services use to talk to each other [D04:1]
- When a request reaches `registry-api`, it first asks `auth-service` to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header before proceeding [D04:2]
- `payments-gateway` checks every request's certificate with `auth-service` before talking to a caller [D09:2]

**From incident data:**
- In **INC-2041**, when `auth-service` was the failed service, only **`billing_agent`** was recorded as affected [D09:2]
- The incident occurred because an intermediate certificate in auth-service expired, causing timeouts that led to billing_agent unable to issue invoices

**Summary:**
- **`billing_agent`** — directly impacted when auth-service fails (due to payments-gateway certificate validation)
- **Any agent using `registry-api`** — indirectly affected since registry-api depends on auth-service for authentication, though this may not have been observed in recent incidents

The billing agent is the most specific agent identified in our records as being affected by auth-service outages. If you need more details about a specific agent's dependency chain, I can search the documentation further.

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

## What the platform is

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.

content.text:
Based on the company documentation, here's what else gets affected when registry-db fails:

## Direct Impacts:

**1. Agent Functionality**
- **`support_agent`**: Sessions begin failing on their first registry lookup. It can't look up agent and account configuration through registry-api anymore [D04:3].
- **`triage_agent`**: Continues running but cannot hand tickets to `support_agent`, causing tickets to queue up (as seen in incident INC-2093, where 212 tickets queued) [D11:1].
- **Other agents**: Any agents that need to look things up in the registry won't be able to complete their tasks [D11:0].

**2. Monitoring & Observability**
- **Overview dashboard**: Goes blank immediately after the failure [D11:1].
- **Monitoring system**: Loses sight of every agent for the same period as the outage. Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds [D04:2].
- This makes it difficult for on-call engineers to identify which agents were actually affected [D11:2].

## Root Cause Chain:
When registry-db becomes unavailable → registry-api can't read/write data → all dependent services fail [D04:2].

This was confirmed during incident **INC-2093** on 2026-08-27, where the 42-minute outage caused these cascading effects across the platform.

- On-call engineering pages are triggered automatically [D11:1]

is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:0" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Overview" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Overview

The Registry API stores the configuration of every agent the company runs: its name, the model it uses, its tier, its owner and its status. Agents and internal tools read it to find out how an agent is configured, and owners write to it to change that configuration. The current version is v2.6.

All endpoints live under one base URL:

```
https://registry.internal.example/v2
```

Requests and responses are JSON. Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC.
</source>

<source id="D01:7" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Tiers and models" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.
</source>

<source id="D01:3" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Reading one agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Reading one agent

`GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id.

```json
{
  "agent_id": "research_agent",
  "model": "claude-legacy",
  "tier": "standard",
  "owner": "research-team",
  "status": "active",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z"
}
```

`GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect.
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="D08:3" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Dashboards

Each agent has a panel with latency, error rate and sessions. The overview dashboard shows every active agent on one screen, sorted by p95. Panels refresh every 30 seconds and lag real time by up to a minute.
</source>

<source id="D08:1" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Alerts" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Alerts

| Alert | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `AgentLatencyHigh` | p95 response time above 8 seconds for 10 minutes |
| `AgentErrorRateHigh` | more than 5% of sessions end in an error over 15 minutes |
| `RegistryUnreachable` | three registry polls in a row fail (`MON-2002`) |

Alerts go to the on-call channel and page the on-call engineer between 08:00 and 20:00. Outside those hours, only `RegistryUnreachable` pages.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:29" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Monitoring Cluster Health" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">

# Cluster size
alertmanager_cluster_members

# Peer health
alertmanager_cluster_peer_info

# Peer position (affects notification timing)
alertmanager_peer_position

# Failed peers
alertmanager_cluster_failed_peers

# State replication
alertmanager_nflog_gossip_messages_propagated_total
alertmanager_silences_gossip_messages_propagated_total
```
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/pushing.md:1" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/pushing.md" title="When to use the Pushgateway" section="When to use the Pushgateway > Should I be using the Pushgateway?" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Should I be using the Pushgateway?

**We only recommend using the Pushgateway in certain limited cases.** There are
several pitfalls when blindly using the Pushgateway instead of Prometheus's
usual pull model for general metrics collection:

* When monitoring multiple instances through a single Pushgateway, the
  Pushgateway becomes both a single point of failure and a potential
  bottleneck.
* You lose Prometheus's automatic instance health monitoring via the `up`
  metric (generated on every scrape).
* The Pushgateway never forgets series pushed to it and will expose them to
  Prometheus forever unless those series are manually deleted via the
  Pushgateway's API.
</source>

## Tiers and models

Every agent has a tier, and each tier allows a fixed set of models:

| Tier | Allowed models |
|---|---|
| `standard` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet` |
| `priority` | `claude-haiku`, `claude-sonnet`, `claude-opus` |

Moving an agent to `claude-opus` therefore means moving it to the `priority` tier first, which needs approval from its owner's budget holder. `claude-legacy` is deprecated and can't be assigned to any agent; existing agents on it keep working until 2026-10-31.

<source id="D01:3" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Reading one agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Reading one agent

`GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id.

```json
{
  "agent_id": "research_agent",
  "model": "claude-legacy",
  "tier": "standard",
  "owner": "research-team",
  "status": "active",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z"
}
```

`GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect.
</source>

## Should I be using the Pushgateway?

**We only recommend using the Pushgateway in certain limited cases.** There are
several pitfalls when blindly using the Pushgateway instead of Prometheus's
usual pull model for general metrics collection:

* When monitoring multiple instances through a single Pushgateway, the
  Pushgateway becomes both a single point of failure and a potential
  bottleneck.
* You lose Prometheus's automatic instance health monitoring via the `up`
  metric (generated on every scrape).
* The Pushgateway never forgets series pushed to it and will expose them to
  Prometheus forever unless those series are manually deleted via the
  Pushgateway's API.
</source>

- Without agent list visibility, engineers couldn't identify which specific agents were affected because monitoring showed "no agents at all" [D11:2]

Based on the incident data we've reviewed, here are the recurring patterns running through our incidents:

## **INC-2041** (April 2026) - billing_agent outage
- **Root cause**: Intermediate certificate in `auth-service` expired at 06:00
- **Impact**: `payments-gateway` timed out waiting for valid certificates; `billing_agent` retried until its step limit ran out
- **Preventive change**: Now alerts 30 days before certificate expiry; `payments-gateway` returns immediate errors instead of hanging

## **INC-2067** (June 2026) - research_agent returning outdated results  
- **Root cause**: Config change increased `kb-search` cache TTL from 7 hours to 7 days without approval
- **Impact**: Cached articles were returned even after updates; policy-based reports quoted outdated information
- **Preventive change**: Cache settings now require Search Team approval for TTL > 24 hours; citations now include article update dates

## **INC-2093** (August 2026) - registry outage during database failover
- **Root cause**: Standby database fell 38 minutes behind primary; monitoring had no alerts for replication lag
- **Impact**: Failover took 42 minutes instead of expected 5 minutes; all agents lost visibility for same period

## **Recurring Patterns:**

1. **Certificate expiration management** - Need proactive cert expiry alerts
2. **Configuration change governance** - Critical parameters like cache TTL require formal approval
3. **Monitoring blind spots** - Services degrading (replication lag) go unmonitored until failures occur

These three incidents show a common theme: **process gaps around configuration changes and infrastructure state monitoring** rather than individual component failures.

### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

### Summary

- If you're collecting and processing hybrid observability data (including metrics _and/or_ events)
- If you're consolidating multiple monitoring tools and need support for metrics _and_ Nagios-style plugins or check scripts
- More powerful event-processing platform

Where Prometheus is better:

- If you're primarily collecting and evaluating metrics
- If you're monitoring homogeneous Kubernetes infrastructure (if 100% of the workloads you're monitoring are in K8s, Prometheus offers better K8s integration)
- More powerful query language, and built-in support for historical data analysis

representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**

Based on the incident data we've reviewed, here are the recurring patterns running through our incidents:

## **INC-2041** (April 2026) - billing_agent outage
- **Root cause**: Intermediate certificate in `auth-service` expired at 06:00
- **Impact**: `payments-gateway` timed out waiting for valid certificates; `billing_agent` retried until its step limit ran out
- **Preventive change**: Now alerts 30 days before certificate expiry; `payments-gateway` returns immediate errors instead of hanging

## **INC-2067** (June 2026) - research_agent returning outdated results  
- **Root cause**: Config change increased `kb-search` cache TTL from 7 hours to 7 days without approval
- **Impact**: Cached articles were returned even after updates; policy-based reports quoted outdated information
- **Preventive change**: Cache settings now require Search Team approval for TTL > 24 hours; citations now include article update dates

## **INC-2093** (August 2026) - registry outage during database failover
- **Root cause**: Standby database fell 38 minutes behind primary; monitoring had no alerts for replication lag
- **Impact**: Failover took 42 minutes instead of expected 5 minutes; all agents lost visibility for same period

## **Recurring Patterns:**

1. **Certificate expiration management** - Need proactive cert expiry alerts
2. **Configuration change governance** - Critical parameters like cache TTL require formal approval
3. **Monitoring blind spots** - Services degrading (replication lag) go unmonitored until failures occur

These three incidents show a common theme: **process gaps around configuration changes and infrastructure state monitoring** rather than individual component failures.

### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:12" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > How to instrument > Subsystems > Failures" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
#### Failures

Failures should be handled similarly to logging. Every time there is a failure, a
counter should be incremented. Unlike logging, the error may also bubble up to a
more general error counter depending on how your code is structured.

When reporting failures, you should generally have some other metric
representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:33" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Common Pitfalls" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:85" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `sqrt()`" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## `sqrt()`

`sqrt(v instant-vector)` calculates the square root of all float samples in
`v`. Histogram samples in the input vector are ignored silently.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:5" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Comparison of Different Solutions" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:84" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Failover" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Failover

Many failover systems use just two systems, the primary and the standby, connected by some kind of heartbeat mechanism to continually verify the connectivity between the two and the viability of the primary. It is also possible to use a third system (called a witness server) to prevent some cases of inappropriate failover, but the additional complexity might not be worthwhile unless it is set up with sufficient care and rigorous testing.

PostgreSQL does not provide the system software required to identify a failure on the primary and notify the standby database server. Many such tools exist and are well integrated with the operating system facilities required for successful failover, such as IP address migration.
</source>

### `<incidentio_config>`

```yaml
# Whether to notify about resolved alerts.
[ send_resolved: <boolean> | default = true ]

# The HTTP client's configuration.

url: <string>
url_file: <filepath>

# The alert source token is used to authenticate with incident.io.
# alert_source_token and alert_source_token_file are mutually exclusive.
[ alert_source_token: <secret> ]

# Alerts exceeding this threshold will be truncated. Setting this to 0
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/configuration.md:153" doc="alertmanager/configuration.md" title="Configuration" section="Configuration > Receiver integration settings > `<incidentio_config>`" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### `<incidentio_config>`

incident.io notifications are sent via the incident.io Alert Sources API.

When configuring this integration, you can do so via the `http_config` by setting the `authorization` directly or using one of `alert_source_token` or `alert_source_token_file`. The configuration of `alert_source_token` or `alert_source_token_file` takes precedence over `http_config`.

Please be aware that if the payload exceeds incident.io's API limits (512KB), the integration will automatically truncate all alerts except the first one.
</source>

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

### Why include unit and type suffixes in metric names?

* **Metric consumption reliability and UX**: When interacting with a modern UI to
use such a metric in PromQL, it's possible to display rich information about the metric's type and unit
(autocompletion, overlays, pop-ups). Unfortunately, interactive, adhoc querying in a powerful UI is not
the only way that users interact with metrics. Metric consumption ecosystem is vast. Majority
of the consumption comes in a form of the plain YAML configuration for variety of observability tools like
alerting, recording, autoscaling, dashboards, analysis, processing, etc. It's **critical**, especially
during monitoring/SRE incident practices to look on PromQL expressions in plain YAML and understand
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:5" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Comparison of Different Solutions" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:84" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Failover" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Failover

Many failover systems use just two systems, the primary and the standby, connected by some kind of heartbeat mechanism to continually verify the connectivity between the two and the viability of the primary. It is also possible to use a third system (called a witness server) to prevent some cases of inappropriate failover, but the additional complexity might not be worthwhile unless it is set up with sufficient care and rigorous testing.

PostgreSQL does not provide the system software required to identify a failure on the primary and notify the standby database server. Many such tools exist and are well integrated with the operating system facilities required for successful failover, such as IP address migration.
</source>

<source id="D13:2" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Why the cap exists" date="2026-09-01" type="official">
## Why the cap exists

In March, a loop bug made `billing_agent` retry failed invoices without a step limit, and it used $2,900 of model calls in one night. The cap limits what any single bug can cost. It isn't a budget target: normal usage is about $2,200 a month.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D13:2" doc="D13" title="billing_agent spend limits and approvals" section="billing_agent spend limits and approvals > Why the cap exists" date="2026-09-01" type="official">
## Why the cap exists

In March, a loop bug made `billing_agent` retry failed invoices without a step limit, and it used $2,900 of model calls in one night. The cap limits what any single bug can cost. It isn't a budget target: normal usage is about $2,200 a month.
</source>

<source id="D05:4" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 4: Check for rate limiting" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 4: Check for rate limiting

Look for `REG-1009` responses in the agent's logs. An agent that's being rate-limited waits for `Retry-After` on every call, which looks like latency. If you find them, check whether another process is sharing the agent's key.
</source>

<source id="D05:3" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 3: Check the cache hit rate" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 3: Check the cache hit rate

If the slow tool is a search, check the cache hit rate on its panel. Below 40% usually means the cache was flushed or restarted, and it refills on its own within about 10 minutes. Wait that long before escalating. If the hit rate stays low after 10 minutes, the cache itself may be misconfigured.
</source>

## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D10:2" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Why it took a week to notice" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

content.text:
Based on our incident records and documentation, here are the recurring causes that run through our incidents:

## **1. Retry Exhaustion & Step Limit Issues**
- **Incident INC-2041**: `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices because payments-gateway timed out waiting for auth-service certificate checks (due to an expired intermediate certificate). The agent treated these as transient errors and kept retrying until it hit its step limit [D09:2].
- **Related Pattern**: A prior bug in March made retries loop without step limits, costing $2,900 overnight from a single loop [D13:2].

**Recurring Cause**: Services timing out instead of returning explicit errors cause cascading retries that exhaust agent capacity.

**Fixes Applied**:
- Auth-service now alerts 30 days before certificates expire
- Payments-gateway returns errors immediately on check failures  
- Billing-agent stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service [D09:3]

---

## **2. Service Dependencies & Authentication Failures**
Multiple agents depend on authentication services before making external calls. When those fail, cascading timeouts occur across the board.

**Key Issue**: Certificate management gaps leave dependent agents vulnerable to sudden failure when auth-services have expired certs.

---

## **3. Registry Outages During Failover**
- **Incident INC-2093**: Database failover caused a 42-minute registry outage because the standby database fell 38 minutes behind. No alert triggered on this lag, so monitoring showed zero agents during the entire period [D11:2].

**Recurring Cause**: Standby lags aren't monitored, causing prolonged outages when they should be brief.

---

## **4. Cache Freshness Blind Spots**
- **Incident INC-2067**: A KB-search config change set cache TTL to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Agents returned stale results silently—the user only noticed later when comparing answers [D10:1].

**Recurring Cause**: Monitoring tracks latency and error rates, but not result freshness or accuracy. Cached responses can drift into correctness issues without triggering alerts.

---

## Summary of Recurring Patterns:
| Pattern | Root Cause | Impact |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Retry exhaustion | Services timeout instead of returning errors | Step limits exhausted, tasks fail |
| Cert expirations | No early warnings for auth-service certs | Cascading failures across agents |
| Unmonitored dependencies | Failovers/lags lack visibility | Extended outages, hard to diagnose |
| Freshness blind spots | No monitoring of data currency | Silent correctness drift |

The fixes implemented show where we've addressed each pattern—better alerts, immediate errors on failure, step limits, and improved dependency monitoring.

Based on our incident records and documentation, here are the recurring causes that run through our incidents:

## **1. Retry Exhaustion & Step Limit Issues**
- **Incident INC-2041**: `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices because payments-gateway timed out waiting for auth-service certificate checks (due to an expired intermediate certificate). The agent treated these as transient errors and kept retrying until it hit its step limit [D09:2].
- **Related Pattern**: A prior bug in March made retries loop without step limits, costing $2,900 overnight from a single loop [D13:2].

**Recurring Cause**: Services timing out instead of returning explicit errors cause cascading retries that exhaust agent capacity.

**Fixes Applied**:
- Auth-service now alerts 30 days before certificates expire
- Payments-gateway returns errors immediately on check failures  
- Billing-agent stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service [D09:3]

---

## **2. Service Dependencies & Authentication Failures**
Multiple agents depend on authentication services before making external calls. When those fail, cascading timeouts occur across the board.

**Key Issue**: Certificate management gaps leave dependent agents vulnerable to sudden failure when auth-services have expired certs.

---

## **3. Registry Outages During Failover**
- **Incident INC-2093**: Database failover caused a 42-minute registry outage because the standby database fell 38 minutes behind. No alert triggered on this lag, so monitoring showed zero agents during the entire period [D11:2].

**Recurring Cause**: Standby lags aren't monitored, causing prolonged outages when they should be brief.

---

## **4. Cache Freshness Blind Spots**
- **Incident INC-2067**: A KB-search config change set cache TTL to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Agents returned stale results silently—the user only noticed later when comparing answers [D10:1].

**Recurring Cause**: Monitoring tracks latency and error rates, but not result freshness or accuracy. Cached responses can drift into correctness issues without triggering alerts.

---

## Summary of Recurring Patterns:
| Pattern | Root Cause | Impact |
|---------|------------|--------|
| Retry exhaustion | Services timeout instead of returning errors | Step limits exhausted, tasks fail |
| Cert expirations | No early warnings for auth-service certs | Cascading failures across agents |
| Unmonitored dependencies | Failovers/lags lack visibility | Extended outages, hard to diagnose |
| Freshness blind spots | No monitoring of data currency | Silent correctness drift |

The fixes implemented show where we've addressed each pattern—better alerts, immediate errors on failure, step limits, and improved dependency monitoring.

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:5" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Comparison of Different Solutions" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:5" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Comparison of Different Solutions" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:76" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:84" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Failover" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Failover

Many failover systems use just two systems, the primary and the standby, connected by some kind of heartbeat mechanism to continually verify the connectivity between the two and the viability of the primary. It is also possible to use a third system (called a witness server) to prevent some cases of inappropriate failover, but the additional complexity might not be worthwhile unless it is set up with sufficient care and rigorous testing.

PostgreSQL does not provide the system software required to identify a failure on the primary and notify the standby database server. Many such tools exist and are well integrated with the operating system facilities required for successful failover, such as IP address migration.
</source>

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:5" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Comparison of Different Solutions" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Comparison of Different Solutions

Shared Disk Failover  
Shared disk failover avoids synchronization overhead by having only one copy of the database. It uses a single disk array that is shared by multiple servers. If the main database server fails, the standby server is able to mount and start the database as though it were recovering from a database crash. This allows rapid failover with no data loss.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:76" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Read-Your-Writes Consistency" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Read-Your-Writes Consistency

In asynchronous replication, there is always a short window where changes on the primary may not yet be visible on the standby due to replication lag. This can lead to inconsistencies when an application writes data on the primary and then immediately issues a read query on the standby. However, it is possible to address this without switching to synchronous replication.

To address this, PostgreSQL offers a mechanism for read-your-writes consistency. The key idea is to ensure that a client sees its own writes by synchronizing the WAL replay on the standby with the known point of change on the primary.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:84" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Failover" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Failover

Many failover systems use just two systems, the primary and the standby, connected by some kind of heartbeat mechanism to continually verify the connectivity between the two and the viability of the primary. It is also possible to use a third system (called a witness server) to prevent some cases of inappropriate failover, but the additional complexity might not be worthwhile unless it is set up with sufficient care and rigorous testing.

PostgreSQL does not provide the system software required to identify a failure on the primary and notify the standby database server. Many such tools exist and are well integrated with the operating system facilities required for successful failover, such as IP address migration.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the incident history, here are the key monitoring gaps that have been exposed:

## 1. **Content Freshness & Accuracy Gap** (INC-2067)
When `research_agent` returned outdated knowledge base articles for seven days, nothing fired in our monitoring systems. The agent's latency and error rate looked healthy because cached answers are fast and never fail. **No standard metric measures whether results are current or accurate** — only manual comparison with the source caught the problem. [D10:2]

## 2. **Full-Stack Outage Visibility Gap** (INC-2093)
During the registry database failover, the overview dashboard went **completely blank**, losing sight of every single agent for 42 minutes. While an alert did fire (`RegistryUnreachable`), the dashboard showing no agent activity made it impossible to gauge the scale of impact. This exposed a critical gap where **monitoring lost visibility into what was actually affected**. [D11:0, D15:1]

## 3. **External Service Timeout Detection Gap** (INC-2041)
When `billing_agent` timed out waiting for responses from `payments-gateway` for 2 hours, the failures weren't evident in our internal monitoring. We saw session failures occurred, but without access to external service health checks, we couldn't identify the root cause from our dashboards alone. This exposed the need for **better visibility into external dependency chains**.

## Summary
These incidents have revealed three core gaps:
- Latency/error rate metrics don't measure result quality or currency
- Full infrastructure outages can blind the entire monitoring stack
- External service dependencies lack visibility in our observability layer

Changes were made after INC-2093 to keep the last good agent list during registry unreachability, fire alerts earlier on standby lag, and make `support_agent` explicitly report registry unavailability instead of failing silently.

Based on the incident history, here are the key monitoring gaps that have been exposed:

## 1. **Content Freshness & Accuracy Gap** (INC-2067)
When `research_agent` returned outdated knowledge base articles for seven days, nothing fired in our monitoring systems. The agent's latency and error rate looked healthy because cached answers are fast and never fail. **No standard metric measures whether results are current or accurate** — only manual comparison with the source caught the problem. [D10:2]

## 2. **Full-Stack Outage Visibility Gap** (INC-2093)
During the registry database failover, the overview dashboard went **completely blank**, losing sight of every single agent for 42 minutes. While an alert did fire (`RegistryUnreachable`), the dashboard showing no agent activity made it impossible to gauge the scale of impact. This exposed a critical gap where **monitoring lost visibility into what was actually affected**. [D11:0, D15:1]

## 3. **External Service Timeout Detection Gap** (INC-2041)
When `billing_agent` timed out waiting for responses from `payments-gateway` for 2 hours, the failures weren't evident in our internal monitoring. We saw session failures occurred, but without access to external service health checks, we couldn't identify the root cause from our dashboards alone. This exposed the need for **better visibility into external dependency chains**.

## Summary
These incidents have revealed three core gaps:
- Latency/error rate metrics don't measure result quality or currency
- Full infrastructure outages can blind the entire monitoring stack
- External service dependencies lack visibility in our observability layer

Changes were made after INC-2093 to keep the last good agent list during registry unreachability, fire alerts earlier on standby lag, and make `support_agent` explicitly report registry unavailability instead of failing silently.

### Administrator's Overview

Advisory locks work normally in recovery, including deadlock detection. Note that advisory locks are never WAL logged, so it is impossible for an advisory lock on either the primary or the standby to conflict with WAL replay. Nor is it possible to acquire an advisory lock on the primary and have it initiate a similar advisory lock on the standby. Advisory locks relate only to the server on which they are acquired.
</source>

## Inhibition

Inhibition is a concept of suppressing notifications for certain alerts if
certain other alerts are already firing.

**Example:** An alert is firing that informs that an entire cluster is not
reachable. Alertmanager can be configured to mute all other alerts concerning
this cluster if that particular alert is firing.
This prevents notifications for hundreds or thousands of firing alerts that
are unrelated to the actual issue.

Inhibitions are configured through the Alertmanager's configuration file.
</source>

### Cascading Replication

To use cascading replication, set up the cascading standby so that it can accept replication connections (that is, set section guc-max-wal-senders and section guc-hot-standby, and configure host-based authentication). You will also need to set `primary_conninfo` in the downstream standby to point to the cascading standby.

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:53" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Cascading Replication" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Cascading Replication

A cascading standby sends not only WAL records received from the primary but also those restored from the archive. So even if the replication connection in some upstream connection is terminated, streaming replication continues downstream for as long as new WAL records are available.

Cascading replication is currently asynchronous. Synchronous replication (see Synchronous Replication) settings have no effect on cascading replication at present.

Hot standby feedback propagates upstream, whatever the cascaded arrangement.

If an upstream standby server is promoted to become the new primary, downstream servers will continue to stream from the new primary if `recovery_target_timeline` is set to `'latest'` (the default).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:52" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Cascading Replication" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Cascading Replication

The cascading replication feature allows a standby server to accept replication connections and stream WAL records to other standbys, acting as a relay. This can be used to reduce the number of direct connections to the primary and also to minimize inter-site bandwidth overheads.

A standby acting as both a receiver and a sender is known as a cascading standby. Standbys that are more directly connected to the primary are known as upstream servers, while those standby servers further away are downstream servers. Cascading replication does not place limits on the number or arrangement of downstream servers, though each standby connects to only one upstream server which eventually links to a single primary server.
</source>

## Failover

Many failover systems use just two systems, the primary and the standby, connected by some kind of heartbeat mechanism to continually verify the connectivity between the two and the viability of the primary. It is also possible to use a third system (called a witness server) to prevent some cases of inappropriate failover, but the additional complexity might not be worthwhile unless it is set up with sufficient care and rigorous testing.

PostgreSQL does not provide the system software required to identify a failure on the primary and notify the standby database server. Many such tools exist and are well integrated with the operating system facilities required for successful failover, such as IP address migration.
</source>

Check its status first: someone may have paused it, or it may have hit a spending cap. Then check whether it's on a model that's being switched off. ## Syntax-checking rules

To quickly check whether a rule file is syntactically correct without starting
a Prometheus server, you can use Prometheus's `promtool` command-line utility
tool:

```bash
promtool check rules /path/to/example.rules.yml
```

The `promtool` binary is part of the `prometheus` archive offered on the
project's download page.

When the file is syntactically valid, the checker prints a textual
representation of the parsed rules to standard output and then exits with
a `0` return status.

If there are any syntax errors or invalid input arguments, it prints an error
message to standard error and exits with a `1` return status.

#### Basic Configuration

Setting `synchronous_commit` to `remote_apply` will cause each commit to wait until the current synchronous standbys report that they have replayed the transaction, making it visible to user queries. In simple cases, this allows for load balancing with causal consistency.

Users will stop waiting if a fast shutdown is requested. ### Administrator's Overview

Advisory locks work normally in recovery, including deadlock detection. Note that advisory locks are never WAL logged, so it is impossible for an advisory lock on either the primary or the standby to conflict with WAL replay. Nor is it possible to acquire an advisory lock on the primary and have it initiate a similar advisory lock on the standby. Advisory locks relate only to the server on which they are acquired.

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:53" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Cascading Replication" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Cascading Replication

A cascading standby sends not only WAL records received from the primary but also those restored from the archive. So even if the replication connection in some upstream connection is terminated, streaming replication continues downstream for as long as new WAL records are available.

Cascading replication is currently asynchronous. Synchronous replication (see Synchronous Replication) settings have no effect on cascading replication at present.

Hot standby feedback propagates upstream, whatever the cascaded arrangement.

If an upstream standby server is promoted to become the new primary, downstream servers will continue to stream from the new primary if `recovery_target_timeline` is set to `'latest'` (the default).
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:52" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Cascading Replication" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
### Cascading Replication

The cascading replication feature allows a standby server to accept replication connections and stream WAL records to other standbys, acting as a relay. This can be used to reduce the number of direct connections to the primary and also to minimize inter-site bandwidth overheads.

A standby acting as both a receiver and a sender is known as a cascading standby. Standbys that are more directly connected to the primary are known as upstream servers, while those standby servers further away are downstream servers. Cascading replication does not place limits on the number or arrangement of downstream servers, though each standby connects to only one upstream server which eventually links to a single primary server.
</source>

## Failover

Many failover systems use just two systems, the primary and the standby, connected by some kind of heartbeat mechanism to continually verify the connectivity between the two and the viability of the primary. It is also possible to use a third system (called a witness server) to prevent some cases of inappropriate failover, but the additional complexity might not be worthwhile unless it is set up with sufficient care and rigorous testing.

## Prometheus Agent Mode

With Remote Write, Prometheus still uses a pull model to gather metrics from applications, which gives us an understanding of those different failure modes. After that, we batch samples and series and export, replicate (push) data to the Remote Write endpoints, limiting the number of monitoring unknowns that the central point has.
