content.text:
Based on the documentation, you get one notification instead of hundreds because **Alertmanager deduplicates alerts** across multiple instances using these mechanisms:

## How Deduplication Works

**1. Alert Grouping**
Alertmanager groups related alerts together based on labels and timing parameters like `group_wait`. This consolidates all failing systems into single alert groups rather than treating each failure as independent. [D07:1]

**2. Notification Log Deduplication**
In HA/clustering mode, Alertmanager uses a shared notification log (`nflog`) that's replicated via gossip between all cluster members. Before any instance sends a notification, it queries this log:
```go
entry := nflog.Query(receiver, groupKey)
if entry.exists && !shouldNotify(entry, alerts, repeatInterval):
    // Skip: already notified recently
    return nil
```

**3. Single-Sender Strategy**
The deduplication logic ensures only one notification is sent per group:
- **First instance (AM-1)**: Checks empty log, sees no recent sends, sends notification, logs entry
- **Subsequent instances (AM-2, AM-3)**: Check log and see the entry, skip notification

This prevents duplicate notifications even if multiple Alertmanager nodes process the same alert simultaneously. [D07:3], [D07:4]

**Result**: Instead of hundreds of individual alerts triggering separate notifications, they're consolidated into alert groups with single, deduplicated notifications delivered to your receivers (Slack, email, etc.).

## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.
</source>

### Metamonitoring

It is important to have confidence that monitoring is working. Accordingly, have
alerts to ensure that Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, PushGateways, and
other monitoring infrastructure are available and running correctly.

As always, if it is possible to alert on symptoms rather than causes, this helps
to reduce noise. For example, a blackbox test that alerts are getting from
PushGateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than individual
alerts on each.

Supplementing the whitebox monitoring of Prometheus with external blackbox
monitoring can catch problems that are otherwise invisible, and also serves as
a fallback in case internal systems completely fail.
</source>

content.text:
You get only one notification instead of hundreds due to two key mechanisms in Alertmanager:

## 1. Grouping (Primary Reason)

Alertmanager automatically groups alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously [D07:2].

For example, if dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your cluster and half can no longer reach the database, alerting rules configured to send an alert for each service instance would result in hundreds of alerts being sent to Alertmanager. Instead, these get grouped together into one notification.

## 2. Deduplication via Notification Log

After grouping, the `DedupStage` queries the notification log to determine if a notification should be sent. It checks:
- Whether firing alerts have changed
- Whether resolved alerts have changed
- Whether the repeat interval has elapsed
- Otherwise, it skips notification (deduplicated) [D06:1]

This ensures you don't get repeated notifications for the same alert group.

Together, these mechanisms prevent notification overwhelm while still keeping you informed about system health issues.

## 1. **Alert Grouping** 
[alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2] - Alertmanager automatically groups alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail simultaneously.

- Groups alerts by cluster+alertname into one group
- Sends that group as a single notification
- Includes details about which instances were affected (you see exactly which services failed, even though it's just one email)

This design ensures you stay informed without being overwhelmed by hundreds of duplicate notifications during major outages.

You only get one notification because **Alertmanager groups and deduplicates alerts** before sending notifications. Here's how it works:

## Why You Get One Notification Instead of Hundreds

During large-scale outages, your Prometheus monitoring system sends an alert for *each individual failing system*. So if 500 service instances lose database connectivity, Prometheus could theoretically send 500 separate alerts.

However, Alertmanager intercepts these alerts and performs several optimizations:

1. **Alert Grouping**: Alerts with matching labels are combined into single notification groups. For example, all alerts where `cluster=my-cluster` and `alertname=DatabaseConnectionFailed` will be grouped together [D07:2].

2. **Deduplication**: Identical or near-identical alerts are consolidated [D07:4].

3. **Notification Consolidation**: Each group results in a single notification, but still includes details about all affected systems within that notification [D08:0].

## Example Scenario

From the documentation: "Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances can no longer reach the database. As a result hundreds of alerts are sent to Alertmanager [D07:2]."

Instead of receiving 500+ emails or Slack messages, you get one notification page showing all 500 affected instances, organized in a readable format.

This design prevents alert fatigue while preserving visibility into what went wrong and which systems were impacted.

<source id="D04:0" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > What the platform is" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## What the platform is

The agent platform is the set of services our agents run on. Agents are configured in the registry, look things up through shared services, and are watched by monitoring. This page describes the core services and how they connect. It doesn't cover every service an individual agent uses; each agent's owner documents those.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/configuration.md:70" doc="alertmanager/configuration.md" title="Configuration" section="Configuration > General receiver-related settings > `<http_config>` (Shared)" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### `<http_config>` (Shared)

An `http_config` allows configuring the HTTP client that the receiver uses to
communicate with HTTP-based API services.
</source>

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D04:0" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > What the platform is" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## What the platform is

The agent platform is the set of services our agents run on. Agents are configured in the registry, look things up through shared services, and are watched by monitoring. This page describes the core services and how they connect. It doesn't cover every service an individual agent uses; each agent's owner documents those.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D12:0" doc="D12" title="Security postmortem SEC-014: registry key written to logs" section="Security postmortem SEC-014: registry key written to logs > Summary" date="2026-07-14" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-07-11, a routine log review found `support_agent`'s write-scoped registry key in plain text in its debug logs. The logs are readable by about 60 engineers. The key was rotated within 3 hours of discovery. The registry's change history shows no use of the key from anywhere other than `support_agent` itself.
</source>

Yes, **technically it's OK for two services to share one registry key**, but there are important considerations:

**How it works:**
- Each registry key gets a rate limit of 60 requests per minute (REG-1009 error occurs when exceeded)
- When two processes share a key, they **share that rate limit**

- **Ownership**: Each key belongs to exactly one agent or person. If two teams need a key, coordinate to ensure clear ownership tracking

**Best practice:**
If the dashboard uses a different read-only key than your agent, they won't interfere with each other's rate limits and maintain clearer ownership boundaries. The FAQ specifically notes you should "give the dashboard its own read-only key" rather than sharing [D14:3].

## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.

## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D05:4" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 4: Check for rate limiting" date="2026-07-09" type="official">

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |

## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

Based on the company documentation, **no, it's not OK for two services to share one registry key.** Here's why:

## Key Reasons

**1. Shared Rate Limits** - Each key has a fixed number of registry calls per minute (60-100 depending on context). When two services share a key, they compete for the same allowance [D01:8][D08:4].

**2. Performance Impact** - If one service makes frequent requests (like a dashboard polling), it can consume most of the quota, leaving little capacity for the other service [D08:4].

**3. Rate Limiting Appearances as Latency** - When a key hits its limit, the next caller gets HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header, which manifests as artificial latency that looks like a performance problem [D05:4].

**4. Audit Ambiguity** - Keys belong to exactly one agent or person, and the registry records who made each change. Sharing keys makes ownership and attribution unclear [D01:1].

## Recommended Practice

> **"If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key."** [D14:3]

You should assign separate keys to different services rather than sharing a single key.

Based on the company documentation, **no, it's not OK for two services to share one registry key.** Here's why:

## Key Reasons

**1. Shared Rate Limits** - Each key has a fixed number of registry calls per minute (60-100 depending on context). When two services share a key, they compete for the same allowance [D01:8][D08:4].

**2. Performance Impact** - If one service makes frequent requests (like a dashboard polling), it can consume most of the quota, leaving little capacity for the other service [D08:4].

**3. Rate Limiting Appearances as Latency** - When a key hits its limit, the next caller gets HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header, which manifests as artificial latency that looks like a performance problem [D05:4].

**4. Audit Ambiguity** - Keys belong to exactly one agent or person, and the registry records who made each change. Sharing keys makes ownership and attribution unclear [D01:1].

## Recommended Practice

> **"If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key."** [D14:3]

You should assign separate keys to different services rather than sharing a single key.

<source id="D14:3" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Why does my agent get told to slow down?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Why does my agent get told to slow down?

Each key gets a fixed number of registry calls per minute. If two things share a key, say the agent and a dashboard, they share that allowance. Give the dashboard its own read-only key.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D08:4" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Polling the registry from your own dashboards" date="2026-03-02" type="official">
## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D04:0" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > What the platform is" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## What the platform is

The agent platform is the set of services our agents run on. Agents are configured in the registry, look things up through shared services, and are watched by monitoring. This page describes the core services and how they connect. It doesn't cover every service an individual agent uses; each agent's owner documents those.
</source>

Based on the internal documentation, **it is not OK** for two services to share one registry key. Here's why:

content.content:
<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

<source id="D06:1" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 1: Issue the new key" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 1: Issue the new key

Issue a key with the same scope as the old one. The old key keeps working, so the agent isn't interrupted.

```bash
regctl keys issue --agent support_agent --scope write
```

`regctl` prints the new key once. Store it in the secrets manager straight away; it can't be shown again.
</source>

<source id="D06:4" doc="D06" title="Runbook: rotating a registry key" section="Runbook: rotating a registry key > Step 4: Revoke the old one" date="2026-07-20" type="official">
## Step 4: Revoke the old one

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

Revoke it within 24 hours of issuing the new one. Leaving both valid for longer doubles the number of keys that can leak. For an exposed key, don't wait: revoke as soon as Step 3 passes.

```bash
regctl keys revoke --key-id <old key id>
```

After revocation, anything still using the old key gets `REG-1003`. That's the signal that something was missed in Step 2.
</source>

<source id="D01:1" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Authentication" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication

Every request must carry a registry key in the `X-Registry-Key` header. A request without one is rejected with `REG-1001`, and a key the registry doesn't recognise is rejected with `REG-1002`.

```bash
curl https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/me \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY"
```

Keys have a scope. A `read` key can call every `GET` endpoint. A `write` key can also create, update and delete agents. Each key belongs to exactly one agent or one person, and the registry records which one made every change. Keys are issued and revoked with `regctl`; see the key rotation runbook.
</source>

<source id="D02:0" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Authentication errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Authentication errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1001` | `MISSING_KEY` | 401 | The request had no `X-Registry-Key` header. |
| `REG-1002` | `INVALID_KEY` | 401 | The key isn't one the registry issued. Check for a truncated or mistyped key. |
| `REG-1003` | `KEY_REVOKED` | 401 | The key was valid but has been revoked. Issue a new key; a revoked key can't be restored. |
| `REG-1004` | `FORBIDDEN_FIELD` | 403 | The key's scope doesn't allow this change. Writes need a `write` key. |
</source>

## Sending alert notifications

Prometheus's alerting rules are good at figuring what is broken *right now*, but
they are not a fully-fledged notification solution. Another layer is needed to
add summarization, notification rate limiting, silencing and alert dependencies
on top of the simple alert definitions. In Prometheus's ecosystem, the
Alertmanager takes on this
role. Thus, Prometheus may be configured to periodically send information about
alert states to an Alertmanager instance, which then takes care of dispatching
the right notifications.
Prometheus can be configured to automatically discover available
Alertmanager instances through its service discovery integrations.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the company documentation for agent latency investigations, here's where slowdowns usually come from:

## Primary Causes

**Most agent latency spikes come from one tool call getting slow, not from the model.** [D05:2]

When investigating an `AgentLatencyHigh` alert (which fires when an agent's p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes), the typical investigation process focuses on:

### 1. Tool Calls (Most Common Source)
- Look at time spent in each tool call and model call in recent slow sessions
- Identify which specific tool got slow and when it started
- This often points to external services or infrastructure issues with the upstream service being called by the agent

### 2. Rate Limiting
- Agents waiting for `Retry-After` on rate-limited calls will appear to have high latency
- Look for `REG-1009` responses in agent logs
- Check whether another process might be sharing the agent's API key [D05:4]

### 3. Cache Issues (for Search Tools)
- For search-based agents, check the cache hit rate
- Below 40% indicates the cache was flushed or restarted and refills on its own within ~10 minutes
- If the hit rate stays low after 10 minutes, the cache may be misconfigured [D05:3]

### 4. Model Calls (Less Common)
- While possible, latency from model inference is less common than tool call latency
- The runbook specifically notes to distinguish between tool and model call timing [D05:2]

When you've identified the slow service, page its owning team with the agent name, the tool involved, start time, and what you've already ruled out before escalating to Platform [D05:5].

Based on the company documentation for agent latency investigations, here's where slowdowns usually come from:

## Primary Causes

**Most agent latency spikes come from one tool call getting slow, not from the model.** [D05:2]

When investigating an `AgentLatencyHigh` alert (which fires when an agent's p95 response time stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes), the typical investigation process focuses on:

### 1. Tool Calls (Most Common Source)
- Look at time spent in each tool call and model call in recent slow sessions
- Identify which specific tool got slow and when it started
- This often points to external services or infrastructure issues with the upstream service being called by the agent

### 2. Rate Limiting
- Agents waiting for `Retry-After` on rate-limited calls will appear to have high latency
- Look for `REG-1009` responses in agent logs
- Check whether another process might be sharing the agent's API key [D05:4]

### 3. Cache Issues (for Search Tools)
- For search-based agents, check the cache hit rate
- Below 40% indicates the cache was flushed or restarted and refills on its own within ~10 minutes
- If the hit rate stays low after 10 minutes, the cache may be misconfigured [D05:3]

### 4. Model Calls (Less Common)
- While possible, latency from model inference is less common than tool call latency
- The runbook specifically notes to distinguish between tool and model call timing [D05:2]

When you've identified the slow service, page its owning team with the agent name, the tool involved, start time, and what you've already ruled out before escalating to Platform [D05:5].

#### Planning for Performance

Synchronous replication usually requires carefully planned and placed standby servers to ensure applications perform acceptably. Waiting doesn't utilize system resources, but transaction locks continue to be held until the transfer is confirmed. As a result, incautious use of synchronous replication will reduce performance for database applications because of increased response times and higher contention.

The section guc-recovery-prefetch parameter can be used to reduce I/O wait times during recovery by instructing the kernel to initiate reads of disk blocks that will soon be needed but are not currently in PostgreSQL's buffer pool. The section guc-maintenance-io-concurrency and section guc-wal-decode-buffer-size settings limit prefetching concurrency and distance, respectively. By default, it is set to `try`, which enables the feature on systems that support issuing read-ahead advice.

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:23" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).
</source>

### Data model

For example, storing the number of HTTP requests to API servers with the
response code `500` and the method `POST` to the `/tracks` endpoint would
commonly be encoded like this in Graphite/StatsD:

```
stats.api-server.tracks.post.500 -> 93

```
api_server_http_requests_total{method="POST",handler="/tracks",status="500",instance="<sample1>"} -> 34
api_server_http_requests_total{method="POST",handler="/tracks",status="500",instance="<sample2>"} -> 28
api_server_http_requests_total{method="POST",handler="/tracks",status="500",instance="<sample3>"} -> 31

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/remote_read_api.md:1" doc="prometheus-server/querying/remote_read_api.md" title="Remote Read API" section="Remote Read API > External labels and remote read" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## External labels and remote read

The `external_labels` setting in `global` affects remote read on both sides:

- **Exposing remote read:** Prometheus appends `external_labels` to every time series returned via `/api/v1/read`. The labels are not stored in TSDB; they are added at response time. Incoming equality matchers that match an external label are rewritten to match the empty string so that TSDB can satisfy the query.
- **Using remote read:** The querying Prometheus sends its own `external_labels` as additional equality matchers in the request, then strips them from the response.
</source>

## Search API

`--enable-feature=search-api`

Enables the experimental search API endpoints for discovering metric names,
label names, and label values with fuzzy matching and filtering support. See
the search API documentation
for details.

The `--web.search.max-limit` flag (default `10000`) bounds the `limit` query
parameter accepted by the search endpoints. Requests with a higher `limit` are
rejected with HTTP 400. The default response limit (100) is silently clamped
to this maximum, so an operator setting a smaller cap does not break
no-`limit` requests. Setting the flag to `0` disables the cap entirely; this
is **not recommended** for endpoints exposed beyond a trusted network because a
single client can then request the entire index in one response.
</source>

## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2" doc="alertmanager/alertmanager.md" title="Alertmanager" section="Alertmanager > Grouping" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the company runbooks and investigation documentation, here's where agent latency slowdowns typically come from:

## Primary Causes (in order of frequency):

### 1. **Slow External Tools/Services** [D05:2]
The most common source of latency spikes is **external tools that get slow**, not the model itself. When you investigate an `AgentLatencyHigh` alert, you should:
- Open recent slow sessions
- Look at time spent in each **tool call** vs each **model call**
- Document which specific tool caused the spike and when it started

Most latency comes from one problematic external service call rather than model inference overhead.

### 2. **Rate Limiting** [D01:8][D05:4]
Agents waiting for **REG-1009** responses due to rate limiting can look like latency:
- Rate limits are **per key, not per agent** (60 requests per minute)
- If multiple processes share the same agent key, they compete for the limit
- Responses include `Retry-After` headers causing the agent to wait
- To diagnose: check agent logs for REG-1009 errors and see if another process is sharing the key

### 3. **Other Common Sources**:
- **Database connections** (PostgreSQL connection pools) - need to track query count and latency
- **Network timeouts** between services
- **API timeouts** on external service calls

## Investigation Approach [D05]:

When investigating a latency spike:
1. **Confirm the issue** on the dashboard (ensure p95 stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes)
2. **Find the slow step** by examining tool/model call timings
3. **Check for rate limiting** in logs for REG-1009 responses
4. **Escalate appropriately** - page the owning team of the slow service, or page Platform if unknown

The key insight: **don't blame the model**. Most latency investigations reveal the culprit is an external tool or service that became slow.

### Data model

For example, storing the number of HTTP requests to API servers with the
response code `500` and the method `POST` to the `/tracks` endpoint would

api_server_http_requests_total{method="POST",handler="/tracks",status="500",instance="<sample1>"} -> 34

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/remote_read_api.md:1" doc="prometheus-server/querying/remote_read_api.md" title="Remote Read API" section="Remote Read API > External labels and remote read" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## External labels and remote read

The `external_labels` setting in `global` affects remote read on both sides:

- **Exposing remote read:** Prometheus appends `external_labels` to every time series returned via `/api/v1/read`. The labels are not stored in TSDB; they are added at response time. Incoming equality matchers that match an external label are rewritten to match the empty string so that TSDB can satisfy the query.
- **Using remote read:** The querying Prometheus sends its own `external_labels` as additional equality matchers in the request, then strips them from the response.
</source>

#### Libraries

Libraries should provide instrumentation with no additional configuration
required by users.

If it is a library used to access some resource outside of the process (for example,
network, disk, or IPC), track the overall query count, errors (if errors are possible)

## Grouping

Grouping categorizes alerts of similar nature into a single notification. This
is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and
hundreds to thousands of alerts may be firing simultaneously.

**Example:** Dozens or hundreds of instances of a service are running in your
cluster when a network partition occurs. Half of your service instances
can no longer reach the database.
Alerting rules in Prometheus were configured to send an alert for each service
instance if it cannot communicate with the database. As a result hundreds of
alerts are sent to Alertmanager.
</source>

Based on the company runbooks and investigation documentation, here's where agent latency slowdowns typically come from:

## Primary Causes (in order of frequency):

### 1. **Slow External Tools/Services** [D05:2]
The most common source of latency spikes is **external tools that get slow**, not the model itself. When you investigate an `AgentLatencyHigh` alert, you should:
- Open recent slow sessions
- Look at time spent in each **tool call** vs each **model call**
- Document which specific tool caused the spike and when it started

Most latency comes from one problematic external service call rather than model inference overhead.

### 2. **Rate Limiting** [D01:8][D05:4]
Agents waiting for **REG-1009** responses due to rate limiting can look like latency:
- Rate limits are **per key, not per agent** (60 requests per minute)
- If multiple processes share the same agent key, they compete for the limit
- Responses include `Retry-After` headers causing the agent to wait
- To diagnose: check agent logs for REG-1009 errors and see if another process is sharing the key

### 3. **Other Common Sources**:
- **Database connections** (PostgreSQL connection pools) - need to track query count and latency
- **Network timeouts** between services
- **API timeouts** on external service calls

## Investigation Approach [D05]:

When investigating a latency spike:
1. **Confirm the issue** on the dashboard (ensure p95 stays above 8 seconds for 10 minutes)
2. **Find the slow step** by examining tool/model call timings
3. **Check for rate limiting** in logs for REG-1009 responses
4. **Escalate appropriately** - page the owning team of the slow service, or page Platform if unknown

The key insight: **don't blame the model**. Most latency investigations reveal the culprit is an external tool or service that became slow.

## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}

</source>

is especially useful during larger outages when many systems fail at once and

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:40" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Asynchronous Commit" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Asynchronous Commit

Asynchronous commit provides behavior different from setting section guc-fsync = off. `fsync` is a server-wide setting that will alter the behavior of all transactions. It disables all logic within PostgreSQL that attempts to synchronize writes to different portions of the database, and therefore a system crash (that is, a hardware or operating system crash, not a failure of PostgreSQL itself) could result in arbitrarily bad corruption of the database state. In many scenarios, asynchronous commit provides most of the performance improvement that could be obtained by turning off `fsync`, but without the risk of data corruption.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:69" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for Performance" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for Performance

Synchronous replication usually requires carefully planned and placed standby servers to ensure applications perform acceptably. Waiting doesn't utilize system resources, but transaction locks continue to be held until the transfer is confirmed. As a result, incautious use of synchronous replication will reduce performance for database applications because of increased response times and higher contention.

PostgreSQL allows the application developer to specify the durability level required via replication. This can be specified for the system overall, though it can also be specified for specific users or connections, or even individual transactions.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:23" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Log-Shipping Standby Servers

Directly moving WAL records from one database server to another is typically described as log shipping. PostgreSQL implements file-based log shipping by transferring WAL records one file (WAL segment) at a time. WAL files (16MB) can be shipped easily and cheaply over any distance, whether it be to an adjacent system, another system at the same site, or another system on the far side of the globe. The bandwidth required for this technique varies according to the transaction rate of the primary server. Record-based log shipping is more granular and streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection (see Streaming Replication).
</source>

Based on the company's documentation, here's where agent latency slowdowns typically come from:

## Most Common Sources

**1. Slow Tool Calls** (Most Frequent)
   - Open recent slow sessions and examine time spent in each tool call versus model call
   - Most latency spikes come from one slow tool, not from the model itself [D05:2]

**2. Rate Limiting**
   - Look for `REG-1009` responses in agent logs indicating the agent was rate-limited
   - When rate-limited, agents wait for `Retry-After` headers, which appears as latency
   - The system lowered the limit to 60 requests per minute per key recently [D03:2], [D05:4]

**3. Database & Service Failures**
   - Database connection timeouts can cause retries until step limits are reached
   - Example: In incident INC-2041, an expired intermediate certificate in auth-service caused timeout and retry loops in billing_agent [D09:2]
   - Service failures propagate through request chains with delays

**4. Network Issues**
   - Network partitions can affect database communication across service instances
   - Hundreds of alerts may fire simultaneously during larger infrastructure outages [alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2]

## Investigation Approach

The recommended process is to follow the "Find the slow step" workflow: identify the specific tool/service causing the latency, then page that service's owning team. If you've ruled out all known causes, escalate to Platform rather than restarting the agent [D05:2], [D05:5].

{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}

Based on the company's documentation, here's where agent latency slowdowns typically come from:

## Most Common Sources

**1. Slow Tool Calls** (Most Frequent)
   - Open recent slow sessions and examine time spent in each tool call versus model call
   - Most latency spikes come from one slow tool, not from the model itself [D05:2]

**2. Rate Limiting**
   - Look for `REG-1009` responses in agent logs indicating the agent was rate-limited
   - When rate-limited, agents wait for `Retry-After` headers, which appears as latency
   - The system lowered the limit to 60 requests per minute per key recently [D03:2], [D05:4]

**3. Database & Service Failures**
   - Database connection timeouts can cause retries until step limits are reached
   - Example: In incident INC-2041, an expired intermediate certificate in auth-service caused timeout and retry loops in billing_agent [D09:2]
   - Service failures propagate through request chains with delays

**4. Network Issues**
   - Network partitions can affect database communication across service instances
   - Hundreds of alerts may fire simultaneously during larger infrastructure outages [alertmanager/alertmanager.md:2]

## Investigation Approach

The recommended process is to follow the "Find the slow step" workflow: identify the specific tool/service causing the latency, then page that service's owning team. If you've ruled out all known causes, escalate to Platform rather than restarting the agent [D05:2], [D05:5].

content.text:
Based on the company's runbooks and incident reports, here's where agent latency slowdowns usually come from:

## Primary Causes

**1. External Tools/Services Getting Slow [D05:2]**
Most spikes come from **one tool that got slow**, not from the model itself. When investigating, you should:
- Open recent slow sessions
- Look at time spent in each tool call and model call
- Write down which specific tool and when it started slowing down

**2. Rate Limiting Issues [D05:4] [D01:8]**
Agents frequently encounter `REG-1009` responses when rate limits are hit (60 requests per minute per key). This is a common cause of apparent latency because:
- Rate-limited agents wait for `Retry-After` headers before retrying
- This can be mistaken for actual slowness
- The issue often happens when multiple processes share an agent's key

**3. Low Cache Hit Rates [D05:3]**
Slow tools (especially search tools) may experience performance drops when:
- Cache was flushed or restarted
- Cache hit rate drops below 40%
- The cache needs ~10 minutes to refill (or longer if misconfigured)

**4. Network/Certificate Issues [D09:2]**
As seen in incident INC-2041, external service failures can manifest as timeouts:
- Intermediate certificates expiring
- Services timing out instead of returning proper errors
- Agents retrying failed connections until they hit step limits

## Investigation Flow

According to the runbook [D05], the typical investigation starts by confirming the latency spike on the dashboard, then finding the slow tool step, checking cache hit rates, and finally escalating to the owning team or Platform if needed.

Based on the company's runbooks and incident reports, here's where agent latency slowdowns usually come from:

## Primary Causes

**1. External Tools/Services Getting Slow [D05:2]**
Most spikes come from **one tool that got slow**, not from the model itself. When investigating, you should:
- Open recent slow sessions
- Look at time spent in each tool call and model call
- Write down which specific tool and when it started slowing down

**2. Rate Limiting Issues [D05:4] [D01:8]**
Agents frequently encounter `REG-1009` responses when rate limits are hit (60 requests per minute per key). This is a common cause of apparent latency because:
- Rate-limited agents wait for `Retry-After` headers before retrying
- This can be mistaken for actual slowness
- The issue often happens when multiple processes share an agent's key

**3. Low Cache Hit Rates [D05:3]**
Slow tools (especially search tools) may experience performance drops when:
- Cache was flushed or restarted
- Cache hit rate drops below 40%
- The cache needs ~10 minutes to refill (or longer if misconfigured)

**4. Network/Certificate Issues [D09:2]**
As seen in incident INC-2041, external service failures can manifest as timeouts:
- Intermediate certificates expiring
- Services timing out instead of returning proper errors
- Agents retrying failed connections until they hit step limits

## Investigation Flow

According to the runbook [D05], the typical investigation starts by confirming the latency spike on the dashboard, then finding the slow tool step, checking cache hit rates, and finally escalating to the owning team or Platform if needed.

### Overview

Prometheus integrates with remote storage systems in four ways:

- Prometheus can write samples that it ingests to a remote URL in a Remote Write format.
- Prometheus can receive samples from other clients in a Remote Write format.
- Prometheus can read (back) sample data from a remote URL in a Remote Read format.
- Prometheus can return sample data requested by clients in a Remote Read format.

The remote read and write protocols both use a snappy-compressed protocol buffer encoding over
HTTP. The read protocol is not yet considered as stable API.

The write protocol has a stable specification for 1.0 version
and experimental specification for 2.0 version,
both supported by Prometheus server.
</source>

## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D15:3" doc="D15" title="Wiki: on-call tips" section="Wiki: on-call tips > Paging etiquette" date="2026-09-20" type="wiki">
## Paging etiquette

When you page another team, say what you've already ruled out. "Registry slow, auth-service latency normal, registry-db CPU at 95%" gets a faster answer than "registry slow, please help."
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="D04:4" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Who to contact" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Who to contact

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.
</source>

<source id="D05:5" doc="D05" title="Runbook: agent latency spike" section="Runbook: agent latency spike > Step 5: Escalate" date="2026-07-09" type="official">
## Step 5: Escalate

If you've found the slow service, page its owning team with the agent name, the tool, the start time and what you've ruled out. If you haven't, page Platform. Don't restart the agent to "see if it helps": a restart drops the sessions in progress and hides the evidence.
</source>

## What happened

- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md:42" doc="prometheus-server/feature_flags.md" title="Feature flags" section="Feature flags > Search API" date="2026-09-26" type="vendor">
## Search API

`--enable-feature=search-api`

Enables the experimental search API endpoints for discovering metric names,
label names, and label values with fuzzy matching and filtering support. See
the search API documentation
for details.

The `--web.search.max-limit` flag (default `10000`) bounds the `limit` query
parameter accepted by the search endpoints. Requests with a higher `limit` are
rejected with HTTP 400. The default response limit (100) is silently clamped
to this maximum, so an operator setting a smaller cap does not break
no-`limit` requests. Setting the flag to `0` disables the cap entirely; this
is **not recommended** for endpoints exposed beyond a trusted network because a
single client can then request the entire index in one response.
</source>

<source id="D15:3" doc="D15" title="Wiki: on-call tips" section="Wiki: on-call tips > Paging etiquette" date="2026-09-20" type="wiki">
## Paging etiquette

When you page another team, say what you've already ruled out. "Registry slow, auth-service latency normal, registry-db CPU at 95%" gets a faster answer than "registry slow, please help."
</source>

## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

## Search API

`--enable-feature=search-api`

Enables the experimental search API endpoints for discovering metric names,
label names, and label values with fuzzy matching and filtering support. See
the search API documentation
for details.

The `--web.search.max-limit` flag (default `10000`) bounds the `limit` query
parameter accepted by the search endpoints. Requests with a higher `limit` are
rejected with HTTP 400. The default response limit (100) is silently clamped
to this maximum, so an operator setting a smaller cap does not break
no-`limit` requests. Setting the flag to `0` disables the cap entirely; this
is **not recommended** for endpoints exposed beyond a trusted network because a
single client can then request the entire index in one response.
</source>

## Packaging and dependencies

Ideally, a client library can be included in any application to add some
instrumentation without breaking the application.

Accordingly, caution is advised when adding dependencies to the client library.
For example, if you add a library that uses a Prometheus client that requires
version x.y of a library but the application uses x.z elsewhere, will that have
an adverse impact on the application?

It is suggested that where this may arise, that the core instrumentation is
separated from the bridges/exposition of metrics in a given format. For
example, the Java simpleclient `simpleclient` module has no dependencies, and
the `simpleclient_servlet` has the HTTP bits.

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

content.text:
Based on the documentation and incident records, here are the agents affected if **registry-api** goes down:

## Direct Impact
- **support_agent** – This agent looks up agent and account configuration through registry-api to answer customer questions. During a registry-api outage, support_agent sessions fail on their first registry lookup and cannot complete tasks [D11:1].

## Indirect Impact  
- **triage_agent** – This agent reads incoming tickets and hands those it can't close to support_agent. Since support_agent becomes unavailable during registry-api outages, triage_agent keeps running but cannot pass tickets over, causing them to queue (e.g., 212 tickets queued during the INC-2093 incident) [D11:1].

## Other Potential Impact
The architecture overview states that **"agents that look things up in the registry"** cannot finish their tasks during registry-api outages [D11:0]. This could include other agents depending on their specific use cases (such as research_agent or notes_agent if they perform registry lookups).

## Summary
The registry-api stores every agent's configuration [D04:1]. When it goes down:
- **support_agent** fails immediately (direct dependency)
- **triage_agent** runs but cannot transfer tickets (blocked by support_agent failure)
- Any agent performing registry lookups will stall their operations

Additionally, the **monitoring service** loses its agent list (refreshes every 30 seconds), meaning it shows no agents until recovery [D04:2].

## Summary

On 2026-07-11, a routine log review found `support_agent`'s write-scoped registry key in plain text in its debug logs. The logs are readable by about 60 engineers. The key was rotated within 3 hours of discovery. The registry's change history shows no use of the key from anywhere other than `support_agent` itself.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">

- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.

<source id="D04:3" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > The agents that use them" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## The agents that use them

`support_agent` answers customer questions. It looks up agent and account configuration through registry-api and searches help articles through kb-search. `triage_agent` reads incoming tickets and hands the ones it can't close to `support_agent`.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D07:1" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Which agents are affected" date="2026-07-02" type="official">

| Agent | Owner | Target model |
|---|---|---|
| `research_agent` | research-team | `claude-sonnet` |
| `notes_agent` | support-team | `claude-haiku` |

Owners can check any agent with `GET /agents/{agent_id}` and look at its `model` field.
</source>

## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

## Summary

On 2026-07-11, a routine log review found `support_agent`'s write-scoped registry key in plain text in its debug logs. The logs are readable by about 60 engineers. The key was rotated within 3 hours of discovery. The registry's change history shows no use of the key from anywhere other than `support_agent` itself.

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D12:1" doc="D12" title="Security postmortem SEC-014: registry key written to logs" section="Security postmortem SEC-014: registry key written to logs > How it happened" date="2026-07-14" type="official">
## How it happened

A developer enabled `REGISTRY_DEBUG=1` on `support_agent` on 2026-06-30 to investigate slow lookups, and didn't turn it off. With that flag set, the registry client logs every request in full, headers included, and the `X-Registry-Key` header is a request header. The key sat in the logs for 11 days.
</source>

Any user with access to the Pushgateway HTTP endpoint can create, modify and
delete the metrics contained within. As the Pushgateway is usually scraped with

create any time series in Prometheus.

administrative HTTP API, which includes functionality such as wiping all the existing
metric groups. This is disabled by default. If enabled, administrative

Ids are case-sensitive. | | `REG-1006` | `AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` | 409 | An agent with this `agent_id` already exists, including a retired one. | | `REG-1007` | `MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED` | 422 | The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model. | | `REG-1008` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | The body is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type. The message names the field. | | `REG-1010` | `MODEL_DEPRECATED` | 422 | The model is deprecated and can't be newly assigned. Currently applies to `claude-legacy`. | ## Reading one agent `GET /agents/{agent_id}` returns one agent's full record, or `REG-1005` if no agent has that id. ```json { "agent_id": "research_agent", "model": "claude-legacy", "tier": "standard", "owner": "research-team", "status": "active", "updated_at": "2026-06-23T09:12:44Z" } ``` `GET /agents/me` returns the agent that owns the key making the request. It's the quickest way to check that a newly deployed key works and belongs to the agent you expect. ### `` [ agent_id: | default = '{{ template "wechat.default.agent_id" . }}' ] [ to_user: | default = '{{ template "wechat.default.to_user" . }}' ] [ to_party: | default = '{{ template "wechat.default.to_party" . }}' ] [ to_tag: | default = '{{ template "wechat.default.to_tag" . }}' ] ``` ## Flags | --storage.agent.path | Base path for metrics storage. Use with agent mode only. | `data-agent/` | | --storage.agent.wal-compression | Compress the agent WAL. If false, the --storage.agent.wal-compression-type flag is ignored. Use with agent mode only. | `true` | | --storage.agent.retention.min-time | Minimum age samples may be before being considered for deletion when the WAL is truncated Use with agent mode only. | `5m` | | --storage.agent.retention.max-time | Maximum age samples may be before being forcibly deleted when the WAL is truncated Use with agent mode only. | `4h` |

## Summary

On 2026-07-11, a routine log review found `support_agent`'s write-scoped registry key in plain text in its debug logs. The logs are readable by about 60 engineers. The key was rotated within 3 hours of discovery. The registry's change history shows no use of the key from anywhere other than `support_agent` itself.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D12:1" doc="D12" title="Security postmortem SEC-014: registry key written to logs" section="Security postmortem SEC-014: registry key written to logs > How it happened" date="2026-07-14" type="official">
## How it happened

A developer enabled `REGISTRY_DEBUG=1` on `support_agent` on 2026-06-30 to investigate slow lookups, and didn't turn it off. With that flag set, the registry client logs every request in full, headers included, and the `X-Registry-Key` header is a request header. The key sat in the logs for 11 days.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/operating/security.md:12" doc="prometheus-docs/operating/security.md" title="Security model" section="Security model > Pushgateway" date="2026-09-23" type="vendor">
## Pushgateway

Any user with access to the Pushgateway HTTP endpoint can create, modify and
delete the metrics contained within. As the Pushgateway is usually scraped with
`honor_labels` enabled, this means anyone with access to the Pushgateway can
create any time series in Prometheus.

The `--web.enable-admin-api` flag controls access to the
administrative HTTP API, which includes functionality such as wiping all the existing
metric groups. This is disabled by default. If enabled, administrative
functionality will be accessible under the `/api/*/admin/` paths.
</source>

Ideally, a client library can be included in any application to add some

## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D03:3" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.3 — 2026-03-10" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.3 — 2026-03-10

- Added the `tier` field to every agent. Existing agents were set to `standard`.
- Each tier now has an allowlist of models. Assigning a model outside it returns `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D02:1" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Request errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Request errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1005` | `AGENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No agent has this `agent_id`. Ids are case-sensitive. |
| `REG-1006` | `AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` | 409 | An agent with this `agent_id` already exists, including a retired one. |
| `REG-1007` | `MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED` | 422 | The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model. |
| `REG-1008` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | The body is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type. The message names the field. |
| `REG-1010` | `MODEL_DEPRECATED` | 422 | The model is deprecated and can't be newly assigned. Currently applies to `claude-legacy`. |
</source>

## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D03:3" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.3 — 2026-03-10" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## v2.3 — 2026-03-10

- Added the `tier` field to every agent. Existing agents were set to `standard`.
- Each tier now has an allowlist of models. Assigning a model outside it returns `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D02:1" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Request errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Request errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1005` | `AGENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No agent has this `agent_id`. Ids are case-sensitive. |
| `REG-1006` | `AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` | 409 | An agent with this `agent_id` already exists, including a retired one. |
| `REG-1007` | `MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED` | 422 | The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model. |
| `REG-1008` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | The body is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type. The message names the field. |
| `REG-1010` | `MODEL_DEPRECATED` | 422 | The model is deprecated and can't be newly assigned. Currently applies to `claude-legacy`. |
</source>
